classification.difficultyReason: Combine successive RHS congruence arguments to establish the included angle needed for a SAS proof.

content.prompt: In the diagram, $AB=BC$, $BE=BD$, $BA$ intersects $DE$ at right angles and $BE$ intersects $AC$ at right angles.

spec.description: Unshaded boundary D–A–E–C–B–D with internal segments AB, DE, BE and AC. F is the intersection of AB and DE; G is the intersection of BE and AC. All seven point labels are retained. The source prints no equality ticks or right-angle marks.
spec.mathematics: AB=BC; BE=BD; AB is perpendicular to DE at F; BE is perpendicular to AC at G.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and point labels are visible; no proof annotations or answers.

answer.short: $\triangle DFB\equiv\triangle EFB$ (RHS): both are right-angled at $F$, $BD=BE$ and $BF$ is common.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle DFB$ and $\triangle EFB$:

$\angle DFB=\angle EFB=90^\circ$ ($BA\perp DE$).

$BD=BE$ (given hypotenuses).

$BF=BF$ (common side).

Therefore $\triangle DFB\equiv\triangle EFB$ (RHS).

answer.short:
$\triangle ABD\equiv\triangle CBE$ (SAS).

Part a gives $\angle DBA=\angle ABE$. Also, $\triangle AGB\equiv\triangle CGB$ (RHS), so $\angle ABE=\angle CBE$. Thus the included angles are equal, with $AB=BC$ and $BD=BE$.
answer.worked:
From part a, $\angle DBF=\angle EBF$ (matching angles of congruent triangles). Since $B,F,A$ are collinear, $\angle DBA=\angle ABE$.

In $\triangle AGB$ and $\triangle CGB$:

$\angle AGB=\angle CGB=90^\circ$ ($BE\perp AC$).

$AB=CB$ (given hypotenuses).

$BG=BG$ (common side).

Therefore $\triangle AGB\equiv\triangle CGB$ (RHS), so $\angle ABG=\angle CBG$. Since $B,G,E$ are collinear, $\angle ABE=\angle CBE$.

Hence $\angle ABD=\angle CBE$.

In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBE$, $AB=CB$, $BD=BE$ and the included angles are equal. Therefore $\triangle ABD\equiv\triangle CBE$ (SAS).
